name: Philip Grant Holladay
race_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic. He identifies with the broad census-style White category and has German and Irish family ancestry.
residence: Philip lives with his wife, Margaret, who goes by Meg, in a single-level ranch house in Sheridan, Wyoming. They moved there in 2019 from the Denver suburbs after he sold his business, partly to be closer to Meg’s older sister and partly because they wanted a smaller town. Their home is comfortable and lived-in, with a converted garage where Philip keeps old sound equipment and recordings. They know a few neighbors well and appreciate being able to reach errands without crossing a large city.
household_income: Their gross household income is typically about $225,000 a year, varying with investment distributions. It comes mainly from investments built from the sale of Philip’s business, his Social Security, and Meg’s public-school pension. They are financially comfortable, with no mortgage, but still consider home upkeep, insurance, future health costs, and how much they want to draw from investments.
children_status: Philip and Meg have no children: no biological, adopted, or stepchildren, and no grandchildren.
education: Philip earned a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from the University of Colorado. He worked with sound equipment while in school and later found that the degree’s grounding in circuits and signal systems was useful, though his eventual success depended as much on customer relationships and learning to manage a small business as on formal engineering.
long_term_goals: He wants to keep traveling while he and Meg both enjoy it, but does not want their calendar to become a race through destinations. He would like to finish organizing a collection of old live-performance recordings and leave a useful selection with the local theater rather than let the tapes sit in boxes. He and Meg also hope to keep their home manageable and remain near her sister. He sometimes talks about spending a month in New Orleans during a music season, but neither has made that a firm plan; Meg is reluctant to leave Sheridan for that long, and Philip has no wish to turn a pleasant idea into an obligation.
occupation: Philip is retired. In his thirties he started a regional live-sound and event-production company, growing it from a small equipment-rental operation into a firm that handled sound for civic events, county fairs, school auditoriums, rodeos, and touring performers. He was hands-on with equipment and troubleshooting, but also spent years hiring crews, negotiating contracts, and smoothing over event-day problems. In his late sixties he sold the company to a group of long-time employees rather than to a larger outside buyer. He helped with the transition, then stepped away from paid work. Now he volunteers about twice a month at Sheridan’s community theater, advising on sound setup and helping preserve a few local performance recordings. He is not responsible for every show and declines requests that would put him back on a regular call schedule.
style: Philip speaks plainly and often illustrates a point with a story about a venue, a customer, or something that went wrong during a show. He is relaxed in an informal conversation and can be animated when talking about live music; in a formal meeting he is more concise and dislikes dressing up a simple point in jargon. He is friendly but not effusive. If a plan seems impractical, he is likely to say so directly, though with Meg he is more apt to explain what he was hoping for before conceding a point.

personality.description: He is resourceful and sociable in settings where people have something concrete in common, but does not seek a crowded social calendar. He likes a capable person and a working solution more than a polished presentation. He can be decisive about technical questions and surprisingly indecisive about small personal purchases. When a trip changes from his original idea, he may grumble briefly before finding something in the alternative plan to enjoy.
personality.big_five_scale: Fictional descriptive ratings on a 1–5 scale, where 1 is low, 3 is moderate, and 5 is high. These are character choices, not measured psychological scores.

preferences.reading: Reading is a regular pleasure, usually over coffee in the morning or for a while before bed. He chooses biographies of musicians and business owners, Western and American history, books about recording and sound, and crime novels with a strong sense of place. He does not insist that leisure reading be educational and will abandon a book that feels like a lecture. He prefers a physical book at home but uses an e-reader on longer trips.
preferences.travel: Travel is important to Philip and Meg, but most of their trips are built around an event, a particular place, or a friend they have not seen in a while rather than a long list of standard attractions. In a usual year they take one trip of roughly eight to ten days and three or four shorter weekends, some centered on live music. They generally travel together. Philip is drawn to how music sounds in a room and how a local scene developed; he enjoys a small venue with a good audience as much as a famous hall. Meg, a retired English teacher, likes historic neighborhoods, bookshops, local history, and having enough quiet time between outings. They make room for both instead of treating one person’s interests as an add-on.
preferences.travel_style_and_tradeoffs: For regional trips they usually drive; for longer journeys they fly, often accepting a connection from Billings rather than making an all-day drive to a larger airport. Philip researches performance schedules and transport, but does not build every hour around a reservation. They prefer a quiet, well-located hotel or inn and will spend on good seats or a performance that matters to them. He has little interest in a luxury label or hotel amenities they will not use. He likes wandering through a neighborhood, stopping for lunch, and leaving a night free after a late show. He no longer enjoys standing through a long performance, so they check whether a venue has seats and manageable access. He likes talking with musicians or sound technicians when the opportunity arises, but does not expect every trip to provide behind-the-scenes access.
preferences.recent_trip: In February 2025, Philip and Meg spent a week in New Orleans. They flew from Billings with a connection, stayed in one hotel, attended two seated performances, and spent time walking through neighborhoods and visiting a small music-history exhibit. Philip had wanted to add several nights in Lafayette to hear more Cajun music. Meg did not want another hotel move and preferred to have unplanned time in the city, so they left the extension for another trip. He was disappointed to miss it, but liked that they could return to a favorite café and did not spend the whole week packing and checking out. One of his favorite moments was a lively early-evening performance they found after Meg suggested they skip a more ambitious late-night outing. He still brings up Lafayette, but does not describe the trip as incomplete.
preferences.other_interests: He likes listening to live recordings at home, taking an easy walk, and meeting one or two former colleagues for lunch. He follows a few musicians and venues but is not constantly checking tour announcements. He enjoys a good meal as part of a trip, not as its central purpose, and has no interest in shopping as a vacation activity.

political_ideology: Moderately conservative. Philip emphasizes tradition, personal responsibility, and limits on government, particularly when he thinks rules make it harder for a small business to operate. He also accepts the value of some public programs, including Medicare, public schools, libraries, and reliable roads. He votes regularly but is not an activist, and does not assume that everyone in his circle shares his politics.
beliefs: He believes people should take responsibility for commitments they make and that a good local institution is worth maintaining. The employee sale of his company reflected his view that the people who had helped build it deserved a real opportunity to own it. He is proud of that decision, though he does not pretend it was the most financially lucrative option available.
skills: Philip is good at diagnosing sound-system problems, understanding how equipment behaves in a real room, and explaining technical matters to people without technical backgrounds. He is an experienced negotiator and has a practical instinct for which parts of an event plan are likely to fail. He can research flights and routes, though Meg is better at finding local cultural listings and keeping track of confirmation details. He is less comfortable with newer audio software than with physical equipment and asks for help when a digital process becomes unnecessarily complicated.
behaviors: He reads most mornings, then checks the local news and weather before deciding whether to walk or run errands. He keeps a modest list of household jobs but is willing to let some wait. For trips, he saves performance schedules and confirmation emails in one place and tends to print a backup itinerary, but usually leaves daytime hours open. He and Meg discuss travel plans over dinner; he may begin with an enthusiastic proposal, while she asks how many hotel changes it involves. At home, he sometimes plays an old recording while sorting through boxes and gets sidetracked listening to the whole performance.
health: Philip has no major health condition that currently prevents ordinary travel or daily activities. He walks comfortably at a relaxed pace, but prolonged standing and steep stairs are tiring, so he favors seated performances and a break after a long day. He drives locally and is comfortable driving familiar regional routes, while Meg usually takes a turn on longer journeys.
relationships: Meg is his closest companion and the person with whom he makes most major decisions. Their marriage is affectionate and companionable; they enjoy traveling together but have different instincts about pace, and neither expects the other to adopt every preference. Meg taught English in public schools and receives a teacher pension. They have no children and are not raising or supporting children. Philip is close to a nephew who lives out of state and exchanges occasional calls with him; Meg’s sister, who lives within driving distance, is an important reason they settled in Sheridan. They have a small circle of friends, including former employees and people from local music and theater groups.
other_facts: Philip keeps a box of old concert programs and a few reels from performances his company recorded, with handwritten notes about rooms and equipment. He has digitized some, but not in any orderly sequence. He is proud that the company he built continued under its employees after he left, and he still enjoys hearing that the business is doing well. He does not want to run it again.
